name: Luna soft-landing failures (E-6, 1963 to 1965)
short_status: Failure, over and over: between January 1963 and December 1965 the Soviet E-6 program ran up eleven straight soft-landing failures, three of them crashing on the Moon (Luna 5, Luna 7, Luna 8), before Luna 9 finally landed on the twelfth attempt in February 1966.

facts.label: The program
facts.value: The E-6 (Ye-6) was Korolev's OKB-1 design for the first lunar soft landing; work began 26 March 1960. The 2.7 m spacecraft massed roughly 1,420 to 1,550 kg and carried a 99 kg airbag-cushioned sealed sphere, the automatic lunar station, identical in concept to the one Luna 9 later landed

facts.label: The losing streak
facts.value: Luna 9 was the USSR's twelfth soft-landing attempt and the first to succeed; the eleven attempts before it, from January 1963 to December 1965, all failed. Six failed at or near launch and five failed in deep space

facts.label: Luna 4 (E-6 No.4)
facts.value: Launched 2 April 1963; a Yupiter astronavigation failure, most likely thermal, stopped the midcourse burn and the probe missed the Moon by about 8,400 km on 5 April before drifting into solar orbit

facts.label: The disguised failures
facts.value: E-6 No.2 reached Earth orbit on 4 January 1963 but its Blok L escape stage never fired; the West catalogued it as Sputnik 25. E-6 No.9 stranded the same way on 12 March 1965 and was masked under the domestic label Kosmos 60. Craft that failed to reach orbit at all (No.3, No.5, No.6, No.8) were never announced

facts.label: Luna 5 (E-6 No.10)
facts.value: Launched 9 May 1965; a flotation gyroscope in the I-100 guidance unit failed, the craft began spinning, and a ground-control error meant the main retro-engine never fired. It crashed on 12 May 1965 at 19:10 UT, the first E-6 to reach the surface

facts.label: Luna 6 (E-6 No.7)
facts.value: Launched 8 June 1965; during the midcourse correction the S5.5A main engine ignited on time but a bad timer command left it firing to propellant depletion, and the probe flew about 160,000 km past the Moon

facts.label: Luna 7 (E-6 No.11)
facts.value: Launched 4 October 1965; the astronavigation optical sensor was set at the wrong angle and lost the Earth during the attitude maneuver, so the retrorockets never fired properly. It crashed 7 October 1965 at 22:08:24 UT in Oceanus Procellarum west of Kepler, near 9.8 N 47.8 W

facts.label: Luna 8 (E-6 No.12)
facts.value: Launched 3 December 1965 and came closest of all: a plastic bracket pierced a landing airbag during inflation, setting the craft spinning at about 12 degrees per second. A nine-second retro burn could not null the velocity, and it crashed 6 December 1965 at 21:51:30 UT near 9.1 N 63.3 W in Oceanus Procellarum

facts.label: The 1958 prehistory
facts.value: The Soviet Moon program's failure streak began even earlier: three E-1 lunar impactors launched on 23 September, 11 October and 4 December 1958 were all lost in flight, the first two when longitudinal resonance shook their R-7 boosters apart and the third to a core-engine shutdown at 245 seconds, before Luna 1 flew in January 1959

facts.label: Luna 5 impact site is disputed
facts.value: Three coordinates exist: 31 S 8 W (the 1965 Soviet announcement, Mare Nubium), a later estimate of 8 N 23 W near Copernicus, and 1.35 S 25.48 W determined by L.V. Ksanfomality in a 2018 Cosmic Research study of the actual impact scar

facts.label: Korolev's death
facts.value: Sergei Korolev, chief designer of the whole Luna effort, died in surgery on 14 January 1966, just 17 days before Luna 9 finally launched and ended the streak he never saw succeed

facts.label: The breakthrough
facts.value: Luna 9 (E-6 No.13) launched 31 January 1966 and soft-landed in Oceanus Procellarum on 3 February 1966, the first survivable landing on another world, closing a campaign in which only Luna 9 and the later Luna 13 succeeded

timeline: Three E-1 lunar impactors are lost in flight, the first two when longitudinal resonance shakes their R-7 boosters apart and the third to a core-engine shutdown; the Soviet Moon program's failure streak begins before Luna 1
E-6 No.2, the first soft-lander attempt, reaches Earth orbit but its Blok L escape stage never fires; it strands in orbit and is catalogued in the West as Sputnik 25
Luna 4 launches; an astronavigation failure kills the midcourse burn and it misses the Moon by about 8,400 km
Two more E-6 craft (No.6 in March, No.5 in April) fail to reach orbit; neither is ever announced
E-6 No.9 is stranded in Earth orbit by another Blok L failure and hidden under the domestic label Kosmos 60; it reenters five days later
Luna 5 launches; a gyroscope fault sets it spinning and the retro-engine is never commanded to fire. It crashes into Mare Nubium on 12 May, the first E-6 to reach the surface
Luna 6 launches; a midcourse engine that will not shut down burns to depletion and the probe flies about 160,000 km past the Moon
Luna 7 launches; its star sensor is set to the wrong angle and loses the Earth before retrofire, and it crashes in Oceanus Procellarum near Kepler on 7 Oct
Luna 8 launches; a bracket punctures a landing airbag and it crashes in Oceanus Procellarum on 6 Dec, the closest miss of the campaign
Luna 9 launches and, on 3 Feb 1966, achieves the first survivable soft landing on another world, ending the streak on the twelfth attempt

coordinates.text: 31.0000°S, 8.0000°W · Mare Nubium (Sea of Clouds): the impact point the USSR announced for Luna 5's 12 May 1965 crash. It is the documented announcement, not a confirmed site: later analyses place the impact near 8 N 23 W, and Ksanfomality (2018) at 1.35 S 25.48 W.
